title: Top Drawing Tablets for Artists (2026)
summary: The Wacom Intuos Pro is the best pen tablet, the Ugee M908 the best budget start, and the Xencelabs Pen Display 16 the best mid-range screen to draw on.
method: Picks come from Creative Bloq's hands-on drawing tablet guide (updated Oct 8, 2026). The Xencelabs Pen Display 16 and Wacom Cintiq Pro 27 are cross-checked against TechRadar's hands-on coverage (June 2025), and the Wacom Intuos Pro against independent 2025 reviews from Photoshop Café and Shutterbug.
assumptions: Prices change often, so we quote only figures the sources show and label them. The Ugee M908, Huion Kamvas 22 (Gen 3) and XPPen Magic Drawing Pad rest on Creative Bloq's testing alone; we found no second independent hands-on review we could use. Sources disagree on whether the 2025 Intuos Pro has multi-touch.

products.name: Wacom Intuos Pro (2025, Medium)
why: Creative Bloq names the redesigned Intuos Pro its best pen tablet overall, praising the solid, slim build, precise tracking and the included Pro Pen 3, which it counts among the best styluses available. Wacom's drivers and app compatibility are the main reason studios keep buying it.
An independent hands-on review from Photoshop Café agrees the 2025 redesign is slimmer and more refined, with mechanical dials replacing the old touch ring and keys moved to the top edge.
specs: Pro Pen 3 with 8,192 pressure levels and tilt (Creative Bloq, Photoshop Café)
USB-C plus Bluetooth 5.3; Photoshop Café reports up to 16 hours of battery life
Comes in Small, Medium and Large; Creative Bloq tested the Medium and recommends Medium or Large
Creative Bloq lists the Medium at $379.95, and its deals box has shown it as low as $299.99 at Amazon; check the current price
pros: Excellent pen feel and the most dependable drivers
Customizable keys, dials and pen buttons
Slim, solid build that should last for years
cons: The most expensive pen tablet Creative Bloq has tested
Only one stylus in the box
Keys now sit along the top, which takes some getting used to (Photoshop Café)
Sources disagree on multi-touch: Creative Bloq lists it, Photoshop Café says it was removed, so confirm before buying
products.best_for: Serious hobbyists and pros who want a tablet that lasts and works with every app
products.skip_if: You are a beginner on a tight budget, where a cheaper tablet gets you drawing for a fraction of the cost

products.name: Ugee M908
why: Creative Bloq calls the Ugee M908 a surprisingly capable budget tablet and the clearest entry point for beginners: a full-size drawing area, a battery-free stylus and eight shortcut keys for under about $50.
It also works with Windows, Mac, Chrome, Android and Linux, so it doubles as a cheap second tablet or a way to draw on a phone.
specs: 10 x 6.25 inch active area, about 495 g
PH23 battery-free stylus, 8,192 pressure levels, 60 degrees of tilt
Eight shortcut keys plus a zoom wheel
Creative Bloq quotes roughly $49 / £40; check the current price
pros: Large drawing area for the money
Shortcut keys and wheel are rare at this price
cons: No Bluetooth or wireless
Slight lag when the pen re-enters hover range (Creative Bloq)
A ridge along the edges may bother some people
Plastic body shows fingerprints
products.best_for: Beginners and anyone who wants to try digital art without spending much
products.skip_if: You want a wireless tablet or a premium build

products.name: Xencelabs Pen Display 16
why: TechRadar's reviewer says the Pen Display 16 is the mid-range tablet he reaches for most. It is light, easy to set up with a single cable, and has a sharp 4K screen with accurate color. Creative Bloq also recommends it, and its deals box features the bundle.
TechRadar argues its 8,192 pressure levels feel more controllable than the 16K of some rivals, and says it undercuts many Wacom displays while matching them on specs.
specs: 16-inch 4K screen, about 275 ppi, 10-bit color
98% Adobe RGB, 98% P3-D65, 99% sRGB (TechRadar)
About 2.67 lb (1.21 kg) and 0.47 in (12 mm) thick
TechRadar lists $999 for the standard kit and $1,249 for the Bundle (stand, Quick Keys remote, USB hub); Creative Bloq's deal box showed the Bundle at $1,061.65 at Xencelabs; check current price
pros: Very light and easy to take on the road
Roomy bezel for resting your wrist
cons: Fewer pressure levels than XPPen and Huion rivals (8,192 vs 16,384), though TechRadar says the difference is hard to feel
Dimmer than the Wacom Cintiq Pro 27: about 300 nits on mains power vs roughly 400
The stand and remote cost extra unless you buy the Bundle
products.best_for: Artists who want a portable 16-inch pen display without paying Wacom Cintiq prices
products.skip_if: You want the biggest possible canvas or on-frame shortcut keys

products.name: Huion Kamvas 22 (Gen 3)
why: Creative Bloq's reviewer calls the Kamvas 22 (Gen 3) a large but not desk-hogging display that pushes into territory once held by pricier rivals. The 21.5-inch screen runs at 90Hz, which Creative Bloq says is unheard of at this size and price.
Huion's pen feels smooth and natural, close to a Wacom Pro Pen 3 in the reviewer's view, and the stand is included in the box, which competitors often charge extra for.
specs: 21.5-inch 2560 x 1440 display at 90Hz
16,384 pressure levels
Dual USB-C and USB-A connections; works with Windows, macOS, Linux and Android
Creative Bloq's price widget showed £599 in the UK; check the current US price
pros: 90Hz screen is unusually smooth for the price
Slim bezels and a sturdy build
cons: No on-frame Quick Keys and no remote included
No touch control
Brightness is solid rather than spectacular
Plastic body, not as premium as a Cintiq
products.best_for: Artists who want a big screen and great value
products.skip_if: You depend on built-in shortcut keys or touch gestures

products.name: Wacom Cintiq Pro 27
why: Creative Bloq names the Cintiq Pro 27 the best pen display for build quality, specs and professional needs, calling out the 4K screen, strong color, and a Pro Pen 3 that feels smooth with excellent tilt and pressure.
On-frame Quick Keys and touch make it feel complete. TechRadar's measurements give it roughly 400 nits of brightness, above the mid-range displays it compares.
specs: 27-inch 4K (3840 x 2160) display, 596 x 335 mm active area
Covers Adobe RGB, P3 and sRGB (Creative Bloq)
Pro Pen 3: 8,192 pressure levels and 60 degrees of tilt
Creative Bloq says prices start at $3,499 / £3,249 and rise with stand bundles; check current price
cons: Very expensive
Heavy, and you need a proper stand, which costs more in the bundle
Overkill for hobby use
products.best_for: Professional illustrators and studios that draw all day
products.skip_if: You are a beginner or hobbyist, where the Kamvas 22 or Xencelabs does far more per dollar

products.name: XPPen Magic Drawing Pad
why: Creative Bloq's best small, budget pen computer: a standalone Android tablet with no computer needed. It has a solid metal body, a micro-textured anti-glare screen that avoids the slippery feel of an iPad, and a stylus the reviewer found accurate.
XPPen updated it in 2025 with the X3 Pro Slim stylus (with tilt) and Android 14, according to Creative Bloq.
specs: Active area about 8 x 5 in (203 x 127 mm), 2160 x 1440 resolution
16,384 pressure levels
Bluetooth 5.1, Wi-Fi, USB-C
Creative Bloq says the price is comparable to a standard iPad; check the current price
pros: Great value for a standalone tablet
cons: Struggles with some demanding paint simulations (Creative Bloq)
The case is not a true protective sleeve
Runs Android, so no Procreate
products.best_for: Artists who want a portable sketchbook for plein-air and sofa drawing
products.skip_if: You need Procreate or a bigger screen; an iPad is better then

tips.title: How to choose
items: Pen tablets are flat and screenless and the cheapest; pen displays let you draw on the screen but cost more; standalone tablets like the XPPen Magic Drawing Pad or an iPad need no computer (Creative Bloq).
Creative Bloq says to look for at least 8,192; TechRadar found it hard to tell 16K from 8K in use, and says higher can even be harder to control.
Check what is in the box.
Stands, shortcut remotes and cables are sometimes sold separately, which changes the real price (Creative Bloq, TechRadar).
For pen tablets Creative Bloq says Medium is the sweet spot; for displays it suggests 16 inches or larger for natural arm sweeps.

faq: A pen tablet is cheaper and easier on your posture but you look at your monitor while drawing. A pen display lets you draw right on the image, which many find more natural but costs more (Creative Bloq).
Is there a good alternative to the Intuos Pro?
Creative Bloq's best-value pen tablet is the Xencelabs Pen Tablet Medium Bundle at $329.99, which adds two pens and a Quick Keys remote.
Can I just use an iPad?
Yes. Creative Bloq's top standalone is the iPad Pro M5, but the Apple Pencil Pro is sold separately and the glossy screen feels slippier than a dedicated drawing tablet.
